39: This plan describes a neighborhood sushi restaurant with a sushi bar in a mid-sized American city of 150,000 to 500,000 people. The space is about 1,800 sq ft (167 sq m), leased as a second-generation restaurant space with a Type I hood and an exhaust duct to the roof, on a street with evening foot traffic. It has a sushi bar in plain view with 10 stools and a refrigerated sushi case, 30 seats at tables ({{aforo}} seats in all) and a to-go packing station by the door. It is run by a single-owner LLC: you as owner and general manager, plus your team, led by a head sushi chef (itamae), the person who runs the bar, buys, breaks down and cuts the fish and signs the menu. Guests are served at the table by W-2 servers, and tips go on top of pay. It opens in January, Tuesday through Sunday for lunch and dinner, and closes on Mondays, Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year's Day.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We average {{clientes_dia}} covers a day across the sushi bar, the tables, take-out and delivery, counting each take-out or delivery order as 1.6 covers, at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days. That produces {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. The average includes the ramp-up from January to April: the Excel spreads the year month by month, and Month 1 is January, the slowest month, so the start falls on the low part of the year. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. It is not a guaranteed return but a starting point: change the assumptions and enter your own numbers.
41: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, sushi bar, refrigeration, hood, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
42: From there, covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, so revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}} in year 1, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the life of the loan, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow in the Excel: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone.
43: You are the owner and the general manager, and the head sushi chef is a hire who leads the bar. With them are a sushi chef, a part-time sushi chef for weekends and dinners, a kitchen line cook for tempura, gyoza and rice, servers who also host and pack to-go orders, and dish and prep help: {{plantilla_puestos}} people counting you, who add up to {{plantilla_jornadas_xl}} full-time equivalents; everyone else is a W-2 employee, and how you pay yourself is a question for your CPA. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-sheet Sushi Restaurant Financial Projections in Excel, the 80-task Sushi Restaurant Startup Checklist, the Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator and the Equivalents Guide. What sets it apart is the cost of every piece: the usable cost per pound of a whole salmon against a fillet, and how many nigiri a pound of raw rice yields, kit estimates that you measure yourself, plus the raw-fish and sushi-rice rules explained in plain English.
46: Not every sushi restaurant is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. The take-out and delivery shop is small, with few seats or none, and lives on marketplaces. The neighborhood sushi restaurant, with a sushi bar and tables plus take-out and delivery, is the model in this plan. The omakase counter, where the chef decides the menu, with about 10 seats, two seatings, a fixed price and reservations, is a different business with different fish. The poke and hand roll bar is a counter service model with no sushi chef at the bar. Kaiten (the conveyor belt) and all-you-can-eat buffets need many more seats at a set price, and franchise kiosks and grocery store sushi are another business again. Each model has its own investment, space and margin, and this plan takes the middle one because it builds a restaurant that is yours.
47: The value proposition is a head sushi chef in plain view and a short menu that does not fill the sushi case with neta (the sliced fish or seafood that goes on the rice), so little of it is thrown away. At the bar, the sushi chef assembles each piece. Sushi rice (shari) is rice seasoned with sushi vinegar (sushi-zu, a mix of rice vinegar, sugar and salt), mixed and cooled in a hangiri, the wooden tub, and measured and made each day. Salmon arrives whole or as a fillet and tuna as saku blocks, the cleaned block ready to slice, and all of it comes with its paperwork or frozen as the Food Code requires. The menu has nigiri (rice with a slice of neta on top), sashimi (sliced fish, no rice), maki (a thin roll with the nori outside), inside-out rolls (rice outside), hand rolls (a cone of nori) and the platter, the tray of mixed pieces that sells best for take-out. A lunch special fills the room at midday.
48: The menu prices to the market rather than to a wish. As a kit estimate based on menus read in mid-sized cities, plus 10 to 20% to bring them to 2026, nigiri runs $5-7 a pair, a classic roll such as the California roll $7-9, a specialty roll $13-18 and sashimi $28-65. The restaurant sells beer, sake and wine only, and the beer and wine license is applied for early and never counted on. Everything is costed piece by piece: with the kit's default values, the calculator shows a salmon nigiri at about 23% food cost and a California roll at about 12%, and that is what lets you price each one fairly and still leave a margin. These are estimates you measure with your own supplier.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per equivalent cover, excluding sales tax, which is {{precio_menu}} with tax, and it comes from three channels. A dine-in guest spends about $36.00 (food $28.50 plus drinks $7.50). A take-out order, at about $41.00 on average, is a platter and an extra or two and works out to about 25 covers a day. A marketplace order, with the menu about 15% higher for about the same basket, is about $46.00 and about 20 covers a day. Dine-in accounts for roughly 70 covers a day. The sales mix is {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverage: drinks are about a fifth of what is sold at the tables and a small share of what goes out the door.
50: One detail saves you a headache: be clear about what you are. This is a neighborhood sushi restaurant with a bar and tables, not an omakase counter or an all-you-can-eat buffet, and you do not need to promise anything exotic to sell it: what counts is clean fish and measured rice. "Sushi-grade" and "sashimi-grade" have no legal definition in the United States, so on the menu and the website say "fish handled for raw service (frozen per Food Code 3-402.11 or exempt, with records)". And do not promise "gluten-free": the bar, the hot kitchen and delivery share surfaces and utensils, and soy sauce and tempura contain wheat.
53: Demand for sushi is better read through what people search for than through market-size estimates of doubtful origin. According to DataForSEO, on October 31, 2026 Google US shows these monthly searches: sushi restaurant 201,000, omakase 201,000, sushi bar 27,100, poke shop 18,100, sushi takeout 9,900 and grocery store sushi 1,900. Read them as interest in the food, not as customers you already have. The one count we cite is IBISWorld's summary: 17,301 sushi restaurant businesses in the United States in 2025, with none holding more than 5% of the market. It tells you the field is crowded and local, which is where an independent can compete.
54: There is a curious gap between the person who eats and the person who opens. Consumers search a lot, but the person about to open searches very little: sushi restaurant business plan gets about 20 searches a month, and how to open a sushi restaurant, sushi business plan and sushi restaurant startup costs get about 10 each. Sushi franchise gets about 260. It is an audience that decides with data and finds almost nothing made for its case. And there is a reason to count on delivery: sushi travels well, rolls and cold platters hold up on the road, and most guests now expect to be able to order it at home.
55: On prices, we read the menus of small and mid-sized cities and added 10 to 20% to bring them to 2026. The kit estimate is nigiri at $5-7 a pair, classic rolls at $7-9, specialty rolls at $13-18 and sashimi at $28-65. Grocery store sushi and kiosks sit below that and anchor the low end of what a guest expects to pay, so compete on visible freshness, the chef at the bar and the menu, not on being the cheapest. The menu prices in the calculator are examples near that band (a little above it on tuna, the piece to watch): replace them with your own.
56: With Month 1 in January and in calendar order, the plan spreads sales with seasonality. December is the peak, with holiday parties and New Year's Eve platters; February rises with Valentine's Day; May rises with Mother's Day and graduations; and January is the slowest month. In a resort or tourist town the summer climbs: change the weights in the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab. Month 1 in January has a consequence: the ramp-up runs from January to April, and the lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, which is why working capital counts.
57: The gap is clear. For how to open a sushi restaurant, the Google results page (the SERP) shows generic restaurant guides from delivery and scheduling software companies, turnkey concept pages, franchise offers, videos and forums. Almost nobody counts the cost of every piece, explains the parasite destruction rule of the FDA Food Code for raw fish, or shows how to hold sushi rice at room temperature with a time limit or a variance.
58: The demand has risks that the plan names. The price of salmon moves the food cost, and the marketplace, with its commission of {{comision_pct}}, eats the margin if you let it grow above the plan's ceiling of {{plataforma_pct}} of sales. Depending on a single fish supplier is a weak point: if it fails, the bar fails. That is why the menu is short, pickup at the restaurant is pushed with price, and it pays to keep a second supplier on hand.
61: Before you set any price, draw a map of who competes with you in your neighborhood. In sushi, competition comes from five sides: neighborhood Japanese restaurants with long menus and buffets, sushi chains and franchises, grocery store sushi and take-out counters, ghost kitchens that sell only through marketplaces, and poke shops, which go after the same lunch guest. Your guests are couples and groups out for dinner, office lunches and weekend families, and they choose on freshness, price and convenience.
62: Porter's five forces look like this at a sushi bar. Supplier power is high: fresh fish depends on a few wholesalers, a failure shows up at the bar right away and the price of salmon moves up and down. Customer power is high, because guests switch restaurants or apps with a click and compare prices. The threat of new entrants is medium: opening looks easy, but the barrier is a space that can take a Type I hood and a head sushi chef who can break down and cut fish. The threat of substitutes is high, with grocery store sushi, poke and ghost kitchens. Rivalry is intense among the long-menu Japanese restaurants and the chains. Your defense is the head sushi chef in view, a short menu and a neighborhood that comes back.
63: Against a franchise, this plan is your own brand, and it pays to run both numbers. A franchise brings a name, suppliers, training and a menu in exchange for a franchise fee and a royalty, and it usually asks for a bigger space than the one in this plan. Ask any franchisor for its Franchise Disclosure Document and read Item 7, the estimated initial investment, and Item 19, if it gives financial performance figures. With your own brand, the investment is {{inversion_total}} and you keep the margin, but you need the head sushi chef. Those figures do not transfer to a different space size: compare the two accounts before you sign.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. Opening means a zoning check, plan review with the health department, a health permit, a building permit and a certificate of occupancy, and the exhaust duct to the roof is the filter for the space: if the building will not allow it, the hot kitchen does not fit. On top of that come the raw fish and sushi rice rules, which you meet with documents and records, and the investment in build-out, sushi bar, refrigeration and hood. Check everything with your city, your county and your health department before you sign the lease.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: clean fish, a steady batch of sushi rice every day and a short menu. In the kit, the calculator compares the usable cost per pound of a whole farmed salmon with a fillet bought clean. The second is the site: a neighborhood with evening life, foot traffic and a space with a hood. The third is cost control: the cost of every piece and the fish yield are measured, not assumed. The fourth is the team: a head sushi chef and a second person who can cut.
66: The SWOT for this concept is clear. Strengths: the head sushi chef in view, a short menu, platters costed by channel and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a space with hood requirements, a single head sushi chef and a cash margin of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even that you have to protect. Opportunities: a product people search for constantly, the lunch special and pickup. Threats: the price of salmon and the marketplace, where the same 24-piece party platter leaves about a fifth less margin than it does dine-in. The defense is two suppliers, costing by channel and a second person who can cut.
69: The marketing strategy starts in the neighborhood and follows the calendar. You open in January, and it helps to be clear about what to expect: the curious arrive in the first month, but regulars and a good rating on the marketplaces take a quarter. That is why the plan does not count on a full room from day one but on a ramp. During that ramp three things matter: the head sushi chef in view, which explains itself from the street, a lunch special that makes it easy to come in at midday, and service that brings people back. Everything else is support.
70: Social media is the shop window of the bar. Post the sushi chef cutting, the nigiri being assembled and the platter heading out the door. Short videos, with the hand that cuts and the piece taking shape in front of the camera, work better on Instagram than menu photos. Show how to order, what is in each roll and what each item is, because that is the part that makes newcomers hesitate. You do not need to post every day: a frequency you can keep is better than a burst followed by silence.
71: Your Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because almost everyone who searches for sushi nearby looks at it, and Yelp is where many guests read before they choose. Complete both with real photos of the bar and the pieces, and keep the hours up to date: Tuesday through Sunday, 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. and 5:00 to 9:30 p.m., until 10:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, without forgetting that you close on Mondays and on Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and New Year's Day. Answer every review, the bad ones too, calmly and in the name of the house. A careful reply reads like a commitment, and it counts for the guest who has not come yet.
72: Local acquisition starts at the door. The midday lunch special is for offices and neighbors, and it is the simple way to fill weekday lunch. Over the year the calendar gives you dates: Valentine's Day in February, Mother's Day and graduations in May, Super Bowl night, and holiday party and New Year's Eve platters by order in December, the peak of the year. To bring people back, keep it simple: your own ordering by phone, text or web for pickup. There is no need to promise conversion numbers that nobody has measured.
73: Marketplace or pickup is a numbers decision. The plan sells {{plataforma_pct}} of its sales through third-party delivery marketplaces and pays a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders. Published plans run from 15% to 30% on DoorDash and on Uber Eats, and Grubhub has its own tiers; promotions and packaging come on top. Your own driver costs wages, employer payroll taxes and auto insurance, and in most states must be a W-2 employee, so check yours. Whatever the channel, the consumer advisory for raw fish goes on your listings there too.
74: Pickup at the restaurant pays no commission, so push it with price. A small discount on a pickup order costs less than the marketplace commission and brings the guest to your door. There is a product problem with delivery too: rolls and cold platters travel well, but tempura and gyoza arrive soft, so on the marketplace they stay off the menu or go in vented containers. That is why the ceiling of the plan is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales through marketplaces. There is no in-house delivery in the plan: if you ever set one up, do it with the numbers above in front of you.
75: The marketing budget of the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for photography, your Google and Yelp profiles, local ads and holiday platters. The brand, the website, the photos and the launch are separate, inside the startup costs ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). Do not spend it all at once: spread the budget along the calendar and keep a part for the slower months.
